o: The process of verifying that software meets requirements and finding defects
items.e: Testing: verification (is it built right) + validation (is the right thing built). Finding defects before production.

items.q: What is the difference between verification and validation?
o: Verification — does it match the specification; validation — does it solve user needs
Verification is manual, validation is automated
items.e: Verification: "Are we building the product right?" — conformance to spec. Validation: "Are we building the right product?" — meeting user needs.

items.q: What are defect, error and failure?
o: Error — a human mistake; Defect — a flaw in the code; Failure — incorrect behavior at runtime
items.e: Error (human) → Defect/Bug (code) → Failure (wrong behavior). One error can spawn several defects; a defect — several failures.

items.q: What are the seven testing principles (ISTQB)?
o: Testing shows presence of defects; exhaustive testing is impossible; early testing; defect clustering; pesticide paradox; context-dependent; absence-of-errors fallacy
Testing guarantees absence of defects; full testing is always possible; QA starts after development; defects are spread evenly; automation solves everything
Testing proves product quality; every scenario must be executed; late testing is cheaper; defects are random; context doesn't affect the approach
Testing replaces requirements review; more tests are always better; one test set works forever; passing tests mean the release is ready
items.e: 7 ISTQB principles: 1. Testing shows presence of bugs 2. Exhaustive testing is impossible 3. Early testing 4. Defect clustering 5. Pesticide paradox 6. Context-dependent 7. Absence-of-errors fallacy.

items.q: What is the pesticide paradox in testing?
o: If the same tests are repeated over and over, they stop finding new defects
Tests that fail for no reason
items.e: Pesticide paradox: the system becomes "immune" to test cases. Tests must be regularly reviewed, updated and extended.

o: 80% of defects live in 20% of modules — the Pareto principle in testing
items.e: Pareto principle: a small number of modules contains most defects. QA focuses on risky areas first.

items.q: What are the levels of testing?
items.e: Levels: Unit (components), Integration (interactions), System (whole system), Acceptance (UAT — business requirements).

o: Testing the smallest units of code (methods/classes) in isolation from dependencies
items.e: Unit tests: fast, isolated, no DB/network. Written by developers. JUnit, TestNG, pytest. The base of the testing pyramid.

o: Testing interactions between components or services
items.e: Integration testing: DB + DAO, Service + Queue, Frontend + Backend. Catches issues at component boundaries that unit tests miss.

o: Testing the fully integrated system as a whole against requirements
items.e: System testing: end-to-end functionality plus non-functional requirements (performance, security). Done by QA on a test environment.

o: Business users verify the system meets their real needs
items.e: UAT: the customer or end users check the system against business requirements. The final gate before production deploy.

items.q: What are alpha and beta testing?
o: Alpha — inside the developer's organization; Beta — by selected end users before release
Alpha is automated; Beta is manual
Alpha is the first sprint; Beta is the second
items.e: Alpha: internal testing by the team. Beta: real users in a real environment. Both happen before the official release.

items.q: What types of testing by purpose exist?
o: Functional, Performance, Security, Usability, Compatibility, Accessibility
items.e: Functional: what the system does. Non-functional: how it does it (performance, security, usability, reliability, scalability).

o: Verifying that new changes didn't break existing functionality
items.e: Regression: after every change (bugfix, feature, refactoring). Automation is critical — manual regression is too slow and expensive.

o: Re-running a previously failed test case after the defect was fixed
items.e: Re-testing: after a developer fix, QA re-runs the exact test case that caught the bug. Unlike regression (broader scope).

o: Testing boundary values: minimum, maximum and the values next to them
items.e: BVA for a 1-100 field: test 0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101. Errors cluster at boundaries. Min, Min+1, Nominal, Max-1, Max is the standard set.

o: Splitting inputs into classes of equivalent behavior — test one value from each class
items.e: EP: 1-100 → classes: <1 (invalid), 1-100 (valid), >100 (invalid). One test per class is enough.

o: A table of all combinations of conditions and the system's corresponding actions
items.e: Decision table: rows = conditions and actions, columns = rules. Guarantees coverage of all combinations. Great for complex if/else business rules.

o: Testing transitions between system states and reactions to events
items.e: State transition: Order (pending → paid → shipped → delivered → cancelled). Test both valid and invalid transitions.

o: Testing user-system interaction scenarios from start to finish
items.e: Use case testing: main flow + alternative flows + exceptions. Ensures coverage of real user journeys.

o: A technique where an experienced tester predicts where bugs may hide based on experience
items.e: Error guessing: experience + intuition → a list of likely defects. Empty fields, null, negative numbers, special characters, large data.

o: A documented set of inputs, preconditions, steps and expected results for a single check
A defect description with actual result, severity, priority, attachments and steps to reproduce
A high-level business requirement without concrete steps or an expected result
An automated script with no preconditions or expected result that just runs in CI
items.e: Test case: Test ID, Title, Preconditions, Steps, Expected Result, Actual Result, Status, Priority. The smallest unit of testing.

o: A set of test cases grouped by functionality or purpose
items.e: Test suite: Login Suite, Checkout Suite, Admin Suite — logical grouping of test cases for easier management and execution.

o: A document describing the scope, approach, resources, schedule and risks of testing
items.e: Test plan (IEEE 829): goal, scope, features to test/not test, approach, entry/exit criteria, resources, risks, deliverables.

o: Conditions that must be met before testing can start
items.e: Entry criteria: build deployed, smoke tests pass, test environment ready, test data prepared. Not met — testing doesn't start.

o: Conditions that define when testing is complete and the release can ship
items.e: Exit criteria: 95% test cases passed, 0 critical/blocker bugs open, coverage > 80%, performance benchmarks met, UAT sign-off.

o: New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retest → Closed (or Reopened)
items.e: Bug lifecycle: New → Assigned → In Progress → Fixed → Ready for Retest → Verified → Closed. Or Rejected/Duplicate/Deferred/Not a Bug.

items.q: What is the difference between severity and priority?
o: Severity — technical impact (blocker/critical/major/minor); Priority — business importance (P1/P2/P3)
Severity defines business urgency; priority describes the technical impact on the system
Severity and priority are always equal, since a critical defect automatically gets top business priority
Priority is set by QA from the stack trace, severity is set by the PM from the release date
items.e: Critical severity + low priority: a crash in a rarely used feature. Low severity + high priority: a typo in the company name on the homepage.

o: Finding the root cause of a defect to prevent it from recurring
items.e: RCA: 5 Whys, fishbone diagram. Not just "where" the bug is but "why" it appeared and how to prevent that class of problems.

o: Simultaneous learning, test design and execution without pre-written cases
items.e: Exploratory: the tester freely investigates the system using experience and intuition. Session-based ET: charters (30-90 min sessions).

o: Prioritizing testing based on the likelihood and impact of risks
items.e: Risk-based: likelihood × impact → priority. Critical functionality + new code + complex logic = highest risk → test first.

o: A source for determining the expected result to compare against the actual one
items.e: Test oracle: specification, user experience, previous version, documentation, domain expert — how we know the expected result.

o: The degree to which a system and its components can be tested effectively
items.e: Testability: observability (we can see the result), controllability (we can control the state), decomposability (we can isolate components).

o: Testing how the system meets requirements: performance, security, usability, reliability, scalability
items.e: Non-functional: Performance (speed), Load, Stress (peaks), Security (vulnerabilities), Usability, Accessibility.

o: Testing integrated into the whole Agile process — QA involved from sprint start, whole-team approach
Testing at the end of the sprint
items.e: Agile QA: three amigos (DEV+QA+BA), TDD/BDD, continuous testing, whole-team quality, refinement participation, in-sprint testing.

items.q: What is the three amigos practice in Agile?
o: BA + Developer + QA discuss a user story together before development for shared understanding
Three testers run regression separately after sprint review and the feature demo
Three test levels: unit, integration and UI, mandatory before every commit
Three quality criteria: speed, design and documentation, checked by the PM after release
items.e: Three amigos: BA explains what is needed, DEV proposes how to build it, QA surfaces edge cases and risks. Prevents misunderstandings.

items.q: What is Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile?
o: A clear checklist for a user story to be considered complete, including testing
items.e: DoD: code review done, unit tests pass, integration tests pass, QA verified, documentation updated, deployed to staging.

o: Specific conditions a user story must satisfy to be accepted — the basis for test cases
Criteria for finishing all release candidate testing after regression and UAT sign-off
Technical requirements for internal implementation, class names, DB schemas and the build pipeline
NFR requirements for performance, security and observability unrelated to story behavior
items.e: AC in Given/When/Then format or a checklist: "Given user is logged in, When clicks logout, Then redirected to login page and session cleared".

o: An approach where Given/When/Then specifications serve as both documentation and automated tests
Testing only UI behavior without business, developers or acceptance criteria examples
Branch-Driven Development, where each user story gets its own git branch and auto-generated tests
Business Data Design, an approach to modeling DB tables before writing API contracts
items.e: BDD (Cucumber, SpecFlow): Given/When/Then scenarios understood by all stakeholders + executed automatically. Living documentation.

o: Red → Green → Refactor: write a failing test first, then minimal code, then refactor
Test After Development: implement the whole feature first, then add tests to confirm it
Testing by a separate QA team after code freeze, when developers have finished
Testing all requirements through the UI before release, regardless of unit tests and code design
items.e: TDD: test → fail (Red) → minimal code → pass (Green) → refactor. Improves code design, 100% coverage by default.

o: Testing at every pipeline stage — from commit to production
items.e: Continuous testing: unit on commit → integration on merge → E2E on deploy → smoke in production. Fast feedback loop.

o: Involving QA and testing as early as possible in the SDLC — starting at requirements
Moving tests to the left in a table
items.e: Shift-left: requirements review, definition of ready, three amigos, TDD. A defect at the requirements stage is ~100x cheaper than in production.

items.q: What is smoke test vs sanity test?
o: Smoke — a shallow check of core functions after deploy; Sanity — a focused check of a specific feature after a fix
Smoke — a detailed check of one bugfix; Sanity — a broad run of critical flows after every deploy
Smoke and Sanity are identical, both mean full regression before a production release
Smoke is run only manually before release; Sanity runs only automatically on every commit
items.e: Smoke: "does it start?" — login, home page, main navigation. Sanity: "does this fix work?" — a narrow check of a specific change.

o: Evaluating how convenient the product is for real users
items.e: Usability testing: can the user complete the task? Learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction (SUS score).

o: Verifying the product is accessible to people with disabilities (WCAG 2.1)
items.e: A11y testing: screen readers, keyboard navigation, color contrast (4.5:1), ARIA labels, alt text. WCAG 2.1 A/AA/AAA. Axe, NVDA, VoiceOver.

o: Verifying the product works across browsers, OSes, devices and resolutions
items.e: Compatibility: cross-browser (Chrome/Firefox/Safari/Edge), cross-OS (Win/Mac/Linux), cross-device (mobile/tablet/desktop).

items.q: What is localization vs internationalization testing?
o: i18n — readiness for localization (dates, currencies, encodings); l10n — translations and cultural specifics
i18n — checking translations for a specific country; l10n — only technical readiness of the code
i18n and l10n are the same, both mean checking grammar and spelling in UI texts
i18n — testing time zones; l10n — checking only date formats without cultural context
items.e: i18n (internationalization): UTF-8, date formats, RTL support. l10n (localization): correct translations, currencies, phone formats.

o: Verifying the system recovers from failures: power loss, network errors, DB crash
Testing backup files without checking system behavior during and after a crash
Testing deployment rollback, only verifying the previous app version comes back
A disaster recovery plan as a document without actually running failure scenarios and checking RTO/RPO
items.e: Recovery testing: how does the system react to a crash? Does it restore state? Show proper messages? RTO/RPO compliance.

o: Automatically injecting small code changes (mutants) and checking whether tests catch them
items.e: Mutation testing (PIT, Stryker): killed mutants / total mutants = mutation score. Reveals weak tests with insufficient assertions.

o: Critical thinking, doubt, hunting for problems, guarding quality — unlike the developer mindset
Optimism about any implementation, happy-path focus and confirming the feature works
Writing tests from a ready-made list without analyzing risks, edge cases and hidden assumptions
Project management, roadmap planning and deadline control instead of exploring product quality
items.e: Tester mindset: "how can this break?" Curiosity, skepticism, systematic approach, attention to detail, advocate for quality.

items.q: What is a test coverage report?
o: A document showing the percentage of code or requirements covered by tests
items.e: Coverage report: statement/branch/path coverage for code (JaCoCo, Istanbul), requirements coverage for functionality.

o: Two testers, or a tester and a developer, test together at the same time
Testing in a pair of browsers
items.e: Pair testing: two participants — one drives, the other observes and suggests ideas. Shares knowledge, finds more bugs, less tiring.

items.q: What is a flaky test and how do you fight it?
o: An unstable test — passes then fails. Fix: isolation, determinism, removing race conditions
A test that consistently fails on every run due to a real defect or a wrong expected result
A test without assertions that always passes and verifies nothing after performing actions
A test with mocks that isolates dependencies and therefore cannot have race conditions
items.e: Flaky tests: race conditions, time dependencies, shared state, network unreliability. Quarantine → analyse → fix → reintegrate.

o: A strategy for preparing, isolating and cleaning up test data
items.e: Test data: factories, builders, fixtures, seed scripts. Isolation — every test gets clean data. Synthetic data for privacy.

o: Verifying the new system version works with data and clients of previous versions
items.e: Backward compatibility: the new API accepts requests from old clients. The new DB schema reads old data. Vital for APIs and mobile apps.
